analysis.one_liner: Opens protected offshore waters to oil and gas drilling and gives tax credits and loan guarantees to nuclear, coal, and pipeline companies.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2008 with zero cosponsors, the bill never received a committee vote and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have lifted a ban on oil and gas leasing in protected areas of the outer Continental Shelf, while letting state governors veto or reshape individual lease sales and splitting the royalties between an energy trust fund and coastal states. It would also have created a nationwide mandate to blend coal-derived fuel into gasoline, diesel, and heating oil starting in 2015, expanded federal loan guarantees for nuclear plants and ethanol pipelines, and added new tax credits for building nuclear plants and the factories that supply them. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain access to offshore areas that had been withdrawn from leasing. Nuclear plant developers and their suppliers would gain a 10 percent construction tax credit, a 20 percent manufacturing tax credit, relaxed federal loan guarantee terms covering up to 80 percent of project cost, cost-shared licensing and design work, federally funded workforce training, and a government working group to promote nuclear exports. Coal companies would gain a guaranteed market: a rising national requirement that motor fuel and other covered fuels contain coal-derived liquid fuel, reaching 6 billion gallons a year by 2022. Ethanol and pipeline companies would gain up to $4 billion in federal loan guarantees for new renewable fuel pipelines. Coastal states would also gain a share of offshore drilling royalties for coastal protection and restoration.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil, gas, coal, and nuclear companies

how_it_helps.text: The bill would revoke the 1998 presidential memorandum that withdrew certain offshore areas from oil and gas leasing, opening those areas to drilling, and would direct the Interior Department to conduct a lease sale in a new producing area [S2][S3].

It would create tax credits for companies: a 20 percent credit for investments in nuclear power manufacturing equipment and a 10 percent credit for construction of advanced nuclear power facilities [S2][S3].

It would relax the terms of the Energy Policy Act of 2005 nuclear loan guarantee program so the government could guarantee up to 80 percent of a facility's cost, and would authorize continued funding of the Nuclear Power 2010 Program, carried out through cost-sharing with the private sector [S2][S3].

It would mandate that covered fuels sold in the United States contain specified and rising volumes of coal-derived fuel from 2015 onward, with facilities capturing at least 50 percent of the carbon dioxide they would otherwise release, creating a guaranteed market for coal-to-liquids producers [S2][S3].

It would direct the Treasury to deposit half of new offshore drilling revenues into a new Energy Independence Trust Fund and half into an account shared with coastal states (75 percent of that half) and the Land and Water Conservation Fund (25 percent), with state money limited to coastal protection, resource mitigation, and related uses [S2][S3].

It would give governors of affected states 60 days to accept, modify, or veto proposed offshore lease sales and development plans near their coasts, and require the Labor Department to run a training program for nuclear industry workers [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would bear the cost of the nuclear tax credits, the risk on expanded loan guarantees for nuclear and pipeline projects, and cost-sharing on new reactor design work. Fuel refiners and importers would face compliance costs from the coal-derived fuel mandate, which would tend to be passed to consumers at the pump and in heating oil. Coastal communities and fisheries would bear the environmental risk of drilling in waters that had been off-limits, in exchange for a share of the royalties. The Treasury would forgo half of the royalties from any new offshore areas.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, fuel consumers, and coastal communities

drawbacks.text: Opening protected outer Continental Shelf waters to drilling exposes coastal fisheries, tourism economies, and shorelines to spill risk; the bill's own mitigation and coastal-protection spending is funded from the royalties that drilling generates, so the protection depends on the drilling happening [S2][S3].
The nuclear loan guarantee changes would let the federal government guarantee up to 80 percent of a plant's cost, putting taxpayers behind private nuclear construction projects if they default [S3].

The coal-derived fuel mandate guarantees coal-to-liquids producers a market of up to 6 billion gallons a year by 2022, embedded in motor fuel and heating oil, even though the required carbon capture threshold is only 50 percent of a facility's own emissions and the fuel's life-cycle emissions need only be no greater than gasoline's [S3].
The tax credits for nuclear manufacturing and construction are direct reductions in federal revenue, and the pipeline guarantee authorization is open-ended ('such sums as are necessary') [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill spreads benefits widely across oil, gas, coal, and nuclear interests while concentrating the costs on taxpayers, fuel consumers, and the coastlines newly opened to drilling. Its genuinely public-facing pieces — a state share of royalties for coastal protection, money for the Land and Water Conservation Fund, a governor's veto over nearby lease sales, and nuclear worker training — are real but modest relative to the industry subsidies and the new drilling exposure. The 50 percent carbon-capture threshold for 'clean coal' fuel and a mandate that only requires life-cycle emissions no worse than gasoline limit its climate value.

outcome.mechanism: Sen. Coleman introduced it on June 12, 2008 and it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day; the committee never took it up, no senator cosponsored it, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Norm Coleman (R-MN) introduced the Energy Resource Development Act of 2008 on June 12, 2008, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance [S1][S5].
The action history shows no further activity after the referral — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote [S5].
The bill expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, no new offshore areas were opened to drilling and no new nuclear, coal, or pipeline subsidies were created; coastal waters, their communities, and taxpayers kept the status quo. Oil, gas, coal, and nuclear companies gained nothing from it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coastal waters and taxpayers; industry gained nothing

for.name: Sen. Norm Coleman
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate; no other senator cosponsored it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance

against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing or markup was ever held, and the bill never reached the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern of support or opposition ever formed.

industries.note: The bill would revoke the 1998 withdrawal memorandum and open protected outer Continental Shelf areas to leasing, directly expanding acreage available to drillers, with leases requiring development within two years or termination. Coastal residents would bear the spill and environmental risk in exchange for a state share of royalties.

industries.industry: Nuclear power plant developers and equipment manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would add a 10 percent construction tax credit for advanced nuclear facilities, a 20 percent manufacturing tax credit, looser federal loan guarantee terms covering up to 80 percent of project cost, continued cost-shared Nuclear Power 2010 funding, federal worker training, and an interagency push to promote nuclear exports. These are direct public subsidies and taxpayer-backed guarantees for a private industry.

The bill would create a renewable-fuel-standard-style mandate requiring covered fuels to contain rising volumes of coal-derived fuel, reaching 6 billion gallons annually by 2022, guaranteeing coal companies a market in motor fuel and heating oil. The cost would flow to refiners and ultimately fuel consumers, while the carbon-capture requirement applies only to the production facility and only at 50 percent.

industries.industry: Pipeline and ethanol/renewable fuel transport companies
industries.note: The bill would authorize federal loan guarantees covering up to 90 percent of the cost of new renewable fuel pipelines, funded by 'such sums as are necessary', shifting construction financing risk onto taxpayers.

industries.industry: Coastal states and local governments (revenue share)
industries.note: New producing states and their coastal political subdivisions would receive a dedicated share of offshore royalties usable only for coastal protection, restoration, hurricane protection, and resource mitigation, and 25 percent of the shared half would go to the Land and Water Conservation Fund. Governors would also gain a 60-day window to veto or modify nearby lease sales. This share exists only if drilling proceeds, tying coastal protection funding to expanded offshore production.
